source_title: Premium: AI Is Getting Way Too Expensive
other_side: Zitron's answer to the enterprise-maturity story is that it is the wrong conversation. He argues that debating what AI does to productivity and jobs distracts from the arithmetic: hundreds of billions of dollars of committed spend against roughly $110 billion of trailing twelve-month revenue across the entire industry, OpenAI and Anthropic included. His central claim is that the longer the bubble inflates the harder the economics get — building and running infrastructure keeps getting more expensive, so hyperscalers and neoclouds must eventually charge considerably more for compute, and the only two customers large enough to buy it are the two that cannot pay. He calls large language models "a definitively niche technology", and on that reading enterprise arguments about token budgets and observability are haggling over a price that has not yet been set honestly.
truth_beneath: Both men are circling one variable: the true unit cost of inference relative to what buyers will actually pay for it. They agree on more than either would admit — enterprise token spend is rising fast, budgets written before the agentic era have been blown, and almost nobody can yet see what their own consumption costs. The empirical question that will resolve is whether inference carries a positive and improving gross margin once depreciation on this capex cycle lands; the observable that settles it is audited lab cost-of-revenue alongside hyperscaler AI segment margins. The residue is pure worldview: whether soaring spend is demand or subsidy. NLW is vindicated if enterprises renew and raise budgets at unsubsidised prices; Zitron is vindicated if renewals shrink the moment prices carry their real cost. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — so the signal is their shared conclusion that cost, not capability, is now the central enterprise question. Watch the first full year of renewals priced to cover depreciation.
